text: The covenants finally fell in 1948, and the decisive case came not from Chicago but from St.
Louis.

In Shelley versus Kraemer, decided May 3, 1948, the Supreme Court held that a court could not enforce a racially restrictive covenant, because using the power of the courts to do so counted as state action barred by the Fourteenth Amendment.
Chief Justice Fred Vinson wrote for the Court, which ruled six to nothing, with three justices stepping aside.
The decision did not erase the racist clauses from the deeds.
Many of those words sit in Chicago property records to this day.
Shelley only made them unenforceable, so a judge could no longer evict a Black family for living where the deed said it must not.
After 1948, Black families finally began crossing into Hyde Park and Kenwood.
The line that the club had drawn in 1908 had held for forty years.
Now it broke.
But the people who had spent decades and dollars holding that line did not simply give up.
They looked for new instruments that the courts would still permit.
Zoning.
Land clearance.
Federal money.
The same university that had funded the covenant defense was already thinking about what to do once the covenants were gone.
The bomb had failed.
The deed had failed.
What came next would be quieter, larger, and backed by the full weight of the government, and it would reshape these blocks far more than any club ever could.
That is the story of the chapter that follows.
